model: Life insurer FCFE at cost of equity, net debt held at zero (engine route)

inputs.sbc_source: FY2025 10-K cash flow statement add-back (MET_Metrics.csv StockBasedComp FY2025 $131M); MET publishes no combined equity-award-tax figure and award-settlement withholding is immaterial against a $2.9bn repurchase programme, so the add-back is used unadjusted
inputs.buyback_note: FY2025 repurchases of common stock $2,883M (financing line; FY2024 $3,207M, FY2023 $3,103M). 9M-2026 $2,128M (Q1 $755M, Q2 $722M, Q3 $651M; 9M-2025 $2,423M), an annualised pace of ~$2.8bn, plus $1,134M of common dividends in 9M-2026: $3.26bn returned against $4.94bn of adjusted earnings to common (66%). The August 2026 $3bn authorisation had $2,972M remaining at 30 September 2026. Buybacks are the mechanism that keeps the count flat and are value-neutral in this model; the FCFE stream is what is capitalised.
inputs.share_count_basis: 628,442,143 common shares outstanding at October 30, 2026 (Q3-2026 10-Q cover) plus 4.9M incremental shares from stock-based awards (Q3-2026 EPS note, treasury-stock method) = 633.3M fully diluted; held FLAT because SBC is expensed in the flows (charged once). Balance-sheet count was 631.1M at 30 September 2026 against 655.3M at 31 December 2025; weighted-average diluted count was 639.9M in Q3-2026 and 673.3M for FY2025. The count is falling ~4-5%/yr on repurchases, which this model does not credit as growth.
inputs.wacc_rationale: Cost of EQUITY 10.25% (was 9.5% at the 2026-10-02 build) for a USD-denominated US life insurer: 10-year UST 5.07% (Yahoo ^TNX, 2026-11-18; monthly closes since August 4.76-5.29%) + 5.0% ERP x beta ~1.05 = 10.3%, rounded to the nearest quarter point. The prior build used a ~4.3% risk-free rate and MetLife's own 2026 outlook assumed 4.40% at December 2026; the 10-year has since moved ~75bp higher and stayed there for three months, which is also what took AOCI from -$18.7bn (30 June) to -$25.3bn (30 September). The same formula is applied at the new risk-free rate rather than re-deriving the method. It is a cost of equity, not a WACC, because the flows are post-interest FCFE (holdco interest paid $903M in FY2025 is inside the adjusted-earnings margin). Same rate in all three scenarios; risk is carried in the driver paths and probability weights, not stacked into the discount rate. If the 10-year returns to ~4.4% the rate goes back to 9.5% and the weighted value rises by roughly $9/share (see reconciliation bridge).
inputs.lease_treatment: Not applicable: operating leases are immaterial for an insurer and are already inside the adjusted-earnings expense base; no lease adjustment in flows or bridge.
inputs.nci_treatment: No deduction. MetLife's adjusted earnings are already AFTER noncontrolling interests: the Q3-2026 10-Q segment note states that adjusted other expenses 'include deductions for net income (loss) attributable to noncontrolling interests and redeemable noncontrolling interests'. The flows are built from adjusted earnings, so the NCI share is already out of them; the prior build's $300M book-value deduction in the equity bridge counted it twice and has been removed (+$0.48/share). NCI was $293M and redeemable NCI (mezzanine) $195M at 30 September 2026; NCI income was $35M in 9M-2026.
inputs.net_debt_treatment: Held at ZERO. Total debt at 30 September 2026 $19.7bn (long-term debt $14,301M, subordinated debt securities $5,145M, short-term debt $289M; a further $254M collateral financing arrangement is excluded) is serviced inside the flows: holdco interest paid is a use of liquid assets inside MetLife's own free-cash-flow definition and interest expense on debt is inside adjusted earnings. Deducting it again after capitalising a post-interest stream would count it twice. The $19.8bn of consolidated cash is almost entirely general-account and subsidiary liquidity backing policy liabilities, not surplus; the $3.4bn of holding-company liquid assets (30 September 2026; $3.6bn at 31 December 2025) sits inside the $3.0-4.0bn buffer management treats as required, so none of it is added as surplus cash.
inputs.notes: MODEL: FCFE at cost of equity on a life insurer, run through the owner-FCF component engine with net debt at zero (the GL / IAG.AX / GMG.AX / CHC.AX cost-of-equity-stream precedent). The dcf-methods routing default for an insurer is BVPS-compounding x exit P/B; overridden because (1) GAAP equity is not a usable compounding base -- it fell from $74.6bn (FY2020) to $29.9bn (FY2022) on the LDTI restatement and the rate-driven AOCI swing (AOCI +$18.1bn at FY2020, -$22.6bn at FY2022, -$18.7bn at 30 June 2026) and it moves by billions a quarter with rates, and (2) MetLife does not compound book: it distributes essentially all holding-company free cash flow (FY2025 $4.4bn returned vs $4.9bn FCF) through dividends and repurchases, and management itself frames value creation as the free-cash-flow ratio (65-75% of adjusted earnings) and the ~$25bn of FCF targeted for 2025-2029. The value driver is therefore the holding companies' free cash flow, i.e. FCFE. ENGINE MAPPING: revenue = total revenues (premiums + policy fees + net investment income + other); ebitda_margin_path = pre-tax adjusted earnings BEFORE stock compensation as % of revenue, with the engine's 21% cash-tax rate reproducing MetLife's adjusted-earnings effective tax rate so that NOPAT = adjusted earnings before preferred dividends (FY2025: $6,137M = 7.96% of revenue; FY2024 $5,996M = 8.45%; H1-2026 $3,276M = 8.57%; base year-1 after-tax margin 8.2% x FY2026 revenue ~$79.7bn gives ~$6.5bn, i.e. ~$9.80 per weighted diluted share against the $9.75 consensus the Analysis cites); sbc_pct_path charges SBC (0.17% of revenue); da_pct_path = 0 (D&A immaterial; capex is not PP&E here); capex_pct_path = capital RETAINED in the insurance subsidiaries (statutory new-business strain, RBC/local capital growth, subsidiary capital contributions and holdco expenses), calibrated so the base-case FCFE to common runs at ~72-73% of adjusted earnings available to common -- inside management's 65-75% two-year-average target and consistent with ~$25bn of FCF over 2025-2029 against ~$34bn of cumulative adjusted earnings, and below the 79-82% actually delivered in FY2024-25 (which included $437M of leverage-neutral debt issuance in FY2025 and ran above target); bull 75-78% (FY2024-25 run-rate sustained), bear 65% (bottom of target); cash_tax_rate_path flat at 21% (adjusted-earnings effective rate; GAAP cash taxes paid were $1,564M in FY2025). PREFERRED STOCK: the flows are BEFORE preferred dividends (adjusted earnings, not adjusted earnings available to common) and the $2,905M liquidation preference of the perpetual preferred (after the $1bn Series redemption in Q3-2025; FY2026 dividend run-rate ~$150M) is deducted once in the equity bridge at liquidation value, which is more conservative than capitalising the ~5.2% coupons at the 9.5% cost of equity. last_fcf = FY2025 free cash flow of all holding companies ($4,890M, MetLife's own definition, after preferred dividends) plus the $194M preferred dividends = $5,084M before preferred, matching the flow basis; reported_fcf = the company-defined $4,890M. An insurer's OCF-less-capex (FY2025 OCF $17,092M) is not free cash, so the owner-FCF identity last_fcf = reported_fcf - sbc - interest_income is deliberately not satisfied here. BVPS cross-check (30 September 2026): GAAP book value per common share ~$30.5 (22,226 - 2,905 preferred over 633.3M), ~$70 ex-AOCI (AOCI -$25,304M); MetLife's own adjusted BVPS (ex-AOCI other than FCTA) runs in the high-$50s to low-$60s, so the current price is ~1.6-1.7x adjusted book against a 15-17% adjusted ROE target -- a cross-check that supports, rather than drives, the FCFE answer. UPDATE 2026-11-19 (Q3-2026 10-Q, filed November 2026): same model, same engine mapping. CHANGED: (a) anchors -- price, share count 640.0M -> 633.3M, balance sheet to 30 September 2026; (b) cost of equity 9.5% -> 10.25% in all scenarios because the 10-year UST is 5.07% against the ~4.3% the prior build used (see wacc_rationale); (c) year-1 margin in all scenarios and years 2-5 in base, year 2 in bull: 9M-2026 adjusted earnings before preferred were $5,061M ($4,939M to common + $122M preferred dividends) on $58,750M of revenue, an after-tax margin of 8.61% against the 8.2% year-1 base; with nine months actual the base FY2026 is now ~$6.73bn (after-tax 8.44%, pre-tax pre-SBC 10.85%, implying Q4 ~$1.67bn, flat on Q4-2025 while 9M ran +15%), bull 10.95%, bear 10.45% (Q4 ~$1.35bn); base years 2-5 are 10.75/10.78/10.82/10.87 (were 10.62/10.70/10.78/10.85), i.e. a step back in FY2027 as above-plan variable investment income normalises, converging on the unchanged path by year 4; (d) the NCI deduction in the equity bridge was a double count and is removed (see nci_treatment). DELIBERATELY UNCHANGED: revenue growth paths in all scenarios (9M-2026 revenue +10.3% YoY is flattered by derivative gains inside GAAP revenue and laps a PRT-heavy Q4-2025 of $23.8bn; FY2026 at +3.4% needs Q4 of ~$21bn, in line with the Q3 run-rate -- a full-year revenue outside $79-81bn would move it); capital retention (capex_pct 2.2% base: 9M-2026 cash returned was 66% of adjusted earnings to common and holdco liquid assets were $3.4bn, inside the 65-75% target and the $3-4bn buffer -- the FY2026 10-K free-cash-flow table would move it); margin years 6-10 and all bear/bull margins beyond the years listed (a change to the 2029 expense-ratio target or a long-term-care reserve charge would move them; the Q3 actuarial assumption review cost only $76M in adjusted earnings); SBC 0.17%, tax 21%, terminal growth and exit caps, the preferred deduction ($2,905M liquidation preference, unchanged), probability weights 25/50/25 and the 15% hurdle. Higher long rates should also lift reinvestment yields over time; none of that is credited beyond the observed year-1 margin, which is conservative given the discount rate has been marked to the same rate move.

equity_bridge.item: Preferred stock at liquidation preference (Series A, D, E, F; perpetual, non-cumulative)
equity_bridge.note: Q3-2026 10-Q balance sheet ($2,905M aggregate liquidation preference, unchanged since the Series G redemption in Q3-2025); flows are before preferred dividends so the claim is deducted once here

historical_growth.growth_rate_source: Base-case ten-year average revenue growth: 3.4% in FY2026 (consensus ~$79.7bn, H1-2026 +6.5% YoY on PRT and Japan), 4.0% in FY2027-28 as adjusted PFOs ex-PRT grow ~5% and net investment income compounds with general-account assets, decelerating to the 2.5% terminal rate; brackets the 2.6-3.9% historical revenue CAGRs
historical_growth.growth_divergence_warning: GAAP equity and GAAP EPS CAGRs are meaningless for MET: the LDTI adoption and the rate-driven AOCI swing took reported equity from $74.6bn (FY2020) to $29.9bn (FY2022), so the 5yr equity CAGR of -17.5% diverges from revenue (+2.6%) by far more than 30%. GAAP EPS (-3.7%/-9.3%) is dominated by derivative and market-risk-benefit marks (FY2025 net income $3.4bn vs adjusted earnings $6.1bn). Growth was selected from revenue history, adjusted PFO growth and management's outlook, not from equity or EPS.
historical_growth.notes: fcf_3yr_cagr and fcf_5yr_cagr are on cash returned to common shareholders (dividends + repurchases: FY2020 $2,808M, FY2022 $4,924M, FY2025 $4,392M) as the only consistently disclosed proxy for distributable FCFE across the window; both are distorted (FY2020 buybacks were paused for COVID, FY2025 capital was diverted to the $1bn preferred redemption and the PineBridge acquisition). MetLife's own holding-company free cash flow was $4,890M in FY2025 and $4,559M in FY2024 (10-K liquidity section); adjusted earnings available to common grew $5.5bn (FY2023) -> $5,796M (FY2024) -> $5,943M (FY2025), a 2yr CAGR of 3.95%, and H1-2026 was $3.2bn vs $2.7bn (+18%). Reported FCF (OCF $17.1bn) is an insurer's operating cash flow and was not used for any CAGR.

base.narrative: Revenue +3.4% in FY2026 then 4% as group benefits and RIS grow adjusted PFOs ~5% ex-PRT and net investment income compounds with the general account, decelerating to 2.5%; pre-tax pre-SBC adjusted margin 10.85% in FY2026 (after-tax 8.44%, nine months actual at 8.61%), stepping back to 10.75% in FY2027 as variable investment income normalises, then rising to 10.95% (after-tax ~8.5%) as the direct expense ratio falls toward 11.3% in 2029 and MIM scales, partly offset by group-benefits pricing competition; capital retention held at 2.2% of revenue (FCFE ~73-74% of adjusted earnings, inside the 65-75% target); tax 21%; terminal at min(Gordon 10.25%/2.5%, 14x FCFE) -- Gordon now binds at ~13.2x.

bull.narrative: New Frontier keeps running ahead of plan: group benefits compounds mid-to-high single digits on voluntary/pet/legal adjacencies, Chariot Re and PRT flow lift RIS, MIM passes $1 trillion AUM with PineBridge, Asia and Latin America grow double digits in local currency, rates hold near 4.4% so spread income and variable investment income run at or above plan, and the expense ratio reaches 11.3% early; after-tax margin reaches ~9.0% and the FCF ratio stays at the 75-78% delivered in FY2024-25; terminal growth 3.0%, cap 16x (Gordon binds at ~14.2x on the 10.25% cost of equity). Year-1 margin 10.95% on nine months actual.

bear.narrative: A rate downcycle and recession: the 10-year falls back toward 3%, compressing RIS/PRT spreads and variable investment income, PRT pricing is competed away by reinsurers and new entrants, group-benefits sales slow with employment and disability incidence rises, a long-term-care reserve strengthening and VA hedge costs land in Corporate & Other, FX (yen, peso) translates earnings lower, and private-credit losses lift the cost of risk; after-tax margin falls from 8.1% in FY2026 (nine months already banked, a weak Q4 of ~$1.35bn) to 7.5% in FY2027 and ~7.1%, regulators keep more capital in the subsidiaries so the FCF ratio sits at 65% (bottom of target), revenue grows ~2%; terminal growth 2.0%, cap 11x.

scenario_narratives.base: MetLife does roughly what its five-year plan says: low-to-mid single-digit revenue growth, an after-tax adjusted margin that holds around 8.4-8.5% on expense discipline and asset-management scale, and about 73-74% of adjusted earnings converted into holding-company free cash flow and returned through dividends and repurchases. Value is the FCFE stream at a 10.25% cost of equity (10-year UST ~5.1%), less the preferred stock at liquidation; GAAP book value, which swings with rates, is a cross-check only. The axes that matter are the level of long rates (spread income, variable investment income), group-benefits underwriting and pricing, PRT and Chariot Re flow, MIM scaling and the expense-ratio glide path, and the legacy long-term care and variable annuity blocks.
scenario_narratives.bull: New Frontier delivers on every pillar at once: group benefits leadership and adjacencies, retirement-platform growth with third-party capital, MIM past $1 trillion AUM, and faster Asia/LatAm growth, in a rate environment that keeps spread and variable investment income full. The after-tax margin reaches ~9% and the FCF ratio stays at the 75-78% delivered in FY2024-25. Even then the exit is capped at 16x FCFE: MetLife is a mature, leveraged life insurer, not a growth compounder.
scenario_narratives.bear: The structural sensitivity the Analysis flags as high severity -- long rates and the legacy LTC/VA blocks -- turns against the company. A rate downcycle compresses spread income and variable investment income, PRT pricing is competed away, a recession slows group-benefits sales and lifts disability claims, LTC reserve strengthening and hedge costs recur, FX and private-credit losses add up, and regulators keep more capital in the subsidiaries. Earnings stall, the FCF ratio sits at the bottom of the 65-75% range, and the stock de-rates to a low-double-digit FCFE multiple.

probability_weighted.weights_rationale: Bear raised from the 15% house default to 25%: the Analysis rates interest-rate sensitivity and the legacy long-term care block as high-severity risks, debt/equity is ~1.8x, and a leveraged spread-based balance sheet has asymmetric downside in a rate-and-credit downcycle. Bull cut from 35% to 25% because it needs several independent things to hold at once -- rates staying near 4.4%, PRT and Chariot Re flow, MIM scaling, the full expense-ratio glide and the FY2024-25 FCF ratio persisting above management's own 65-75% target. Base 50%: the plan is running ahead of schedule (Q2-2026 adjusted ROE 17%, adjusted EPS +20%) and the base case already credits that.

valuation_philosophy.summary: MetLife is valued as the present value of the free cash flow its holding companies can actually extract -- dividends and returns of capital from the insurance and asset-management subsidiaries after statutory capital retention, holding-company interest and expenses -- discounted at a 10.25% cost of equity over a ten-year explicit horizon, with the perpetual preferred stock deducted at its $2.9bn liquidation preference and no separate net-debt deduction because the ~$20bn of holdco debt is serviced inside the flows. The flow is calibrated to MetLife's own disclosed free cash flow ($4.9bn FY2025, $4.6bn FY2024; 65-75% two-year-average target; ~$25bn planned for 2025-2029), not to GAAP operating cash flow or GAAP book value, both of which are meaningless for a life insurer under LDTI. The terminal value is capped at 14x FCFE in base (11x bear, 16x bull). Buybacks are not credited as growth: the share count is held flat at 633M and the double-digit adjusted EPS growth management targets is, in this model, mostly the FCFE being returned rather than value created.
key_risks_to_valuation: Capital-retention assumption (capex_pct 2.2% of revenue in base, i.e. FCFE ~73-74% of adjusted earnings) is the single most important driver: every 10pp of FCF ratio is worth roughly $12-15/share; it is calibrated to management's 65-75% target and the ~$25bn 2025-29 plan, below the 79-82% delivered in FY2024-25
Discount-rate sensitivity: each 25bp of cost of equity is worth roughly $3/share of weighted value; the 75bp increase at this update is the single largest item in the reconciliation bridge

Interest rates cut both ways: the 10-year at ~5.1% has taken the cost of equity to 10.25% (about -$9/share against the prior 9.5%) and AOCI to -$25.3bn, while the earnings benefit of higher reinvestment yields is credited only through the observed FY2026 margin; a sustained move back toward 3% lowers the discount rate but compresses RIS/PRT spreads and variable investment income (the bear case). AOCI does not affect the FCFE stream unless bonds are sold

Legacy long-term care and variable annuity blocks in Corporate & Other: a reserve strengthening or hedge-cost spike lands directly in adjusted earnings and is modelled only in the bear case beyond the ~$290M/yr Corporate & Other drag inside the base margin
Adjusted earnings include ~$1.6bn (pre-tax) of assumed variable investment income in 2026; private equity returns below the 9% assumption push the after-tax margin below the 8.4% base year-1 level

Group benefits (28% of adjusted earnings) is a commoditised renewal market; a pricing cycle or adverse mortality/morbidity moves the margin by tens of basis points, which is material on a ~8% after-tax margin
FX translation of Japan, Mexico and Chile earnings (Asia + LatAm = 41% of FY2025 adjusted earnings) and emerging-market regulatory risk

Revenue is lumpy (jumbo pension risk transfers book as premiums: FY2025 +8.6%); the margin-on-revenue construction means a PRT-heavy year inflates revenue and dilutes the margin without changing FCFE, so year-to-year comparisons of the driver paths should be made on adjusted earnings, not revenue
